questions.q: Two point charges are separated by a distance $r$ in a medium of dielectric constant $K$. The force between them compared with that in vacuum is:
questions.solution:
$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 K}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^{2}}$.

The medium's molecules polarise and partly screen the charges, so the force is **$K$ times smaller** than in vacuum.

For water $K \approx 80$, which is why ionic salts dissolve so readily in it.

questions.q: The electric field inside a hollow charged conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is:
questions.solution:
In electrostatic equilibrium all the excess charge resides on the outer surface and the field inside the conducting material — and inside an empty cavity — is **zero**.

If it were not, free electrons would move until it was. This is electrostatic shielding, the principle of the Faraday cage, and why a car is a safe place in a lightning storm.

questions.q: Gauss's law states that the flux through a closed surface equals:
questions.solution:
$\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \mathbf{\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}}$.

Only the charge **enclosed** counts; charges outside contribute equal inward and outward flux that cancels. Choosing a surface that matches the symmetry of the charge distribution is what makes the law a calculating tool.

questions.q: Three capacitors each of capacitance $C$ are connected in series. The equivalent capacitance is:
questions.solution:
In series the reciprocals add:

$\dfrac{1}{C_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{C} + \dfrac{1}{C} + \dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{3}{C}$

$C_{eq} = \mathbf{C/3}$.

Capacitors behave the opposite way round to resistors: series **reduces** capacitance, parallel adds it.

questions.q: The work done in moving a charge between two points on the same equipotential surface is:
questions.solution:
$W = q\,\Delta V$, and on an equipotential surface $\Delta V = 0$, so $W = \mathbf{0}$.

It follows that the field is always **perpendicular** to an equipotential surface — a component along it would do work on a charge moving there.

questions.q: The torque on an electric dipole of moment $p$ in a uniform field $E$ is:
questions.solution:
$\vec{\tau} = \vec{p}\times\vec{E}$, so the magnitude is $\mathbf{pE\sin\theta}$.

The torque is greatest when the dipole is perpendicular to the field and zero when it is aligned — which is the stable equilibrium.

In a *uniform* field the net **force** is zero, so the dipole rotates without translating.

questions.q: The energy stored in a capacitor of capacitance $C$ charged to potential $V$ is:
questions.solution:
$U = \mathbf{\tfrac{1}{2}CV^{2}}$, with the equivalent forms $\dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C}$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}QV$.

The factor of a half arises because the potential rises from $0$ to $V$ as the capacitor charges — the *average* potential through which charge is carried is $V/2$.

questions.q: The electric field due to an infinite sheet of charge with surface density $\sigma$ is:
questions.solution:
Taking a cylindrical Gaussian surface through the sheet, flux emerges from **both** end faces:

$2EA = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow E = \mathbf{\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}}$

Notice it is **independent of distance** — the field of an infinite sheet is uniform.

(A conducting surface gives $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, because there the field exists on one side only.)

questions.q: Compared with the gravitational force between two protons, the electrostatic force is:
questions.solution:
Both forces obey an inverse-square law, so the ratio is independent of separation:

$\dfrac{F_e}{F_g} = \dfrac{ke^{2}}{Gm_p^{2}} \approx \mathbf{10^{36}}$

Gravity dominates on astronomical scales only because bulk matter is electrically neutral — the far stronger electrical forces cancel out, while mass always adds.

questions.q: Two charges of $2\ \mu\text{C}$ and $3\ \mu\text{C}$ are $0.3\ \text{m}$ apart in vacuum. Taking $k = 9\times10^{9}$ SI units, find the force between them, in newtons.
A $10\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is charged to $100\ \text{V}$. Find the energy stored, in joules.
Find the potential, in volts, at a distance $0.3\ \text{m}$ from a point charge of $3\ \text{nC}$. Take $k = 9\times10^{9}$ SI units.
Capacitors of $2\ \mu\text{F}$ and $3\ \mu\text{F}$ are connected in series. Find the equivalent capacitance, in microfarads, to two decimal places.
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{1}{C_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{3 + 2}{6} = \dfrac{5}{6}$

$C_{eq} = \dfrac{6}{5} = \mathbf{1.2\ \mu\text{F}}$.

As always in series, the result is smaller than either capacitor.

questions.q: A charge of $8.85\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}$ is enclosed by a closed surface. Taking $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^{2}N^{-1}m^{-2}}$, find the electric flux, in $\mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}$.
questions.solution:
$\Phi = \dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{8.85\times10^{-12}}{8.85\times10^{-12}} = \mathbf{1\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}}$.

The shape of the surface is irrelevant — only the enclosed charge matters.

questions.q: Using Gauss's law, derive the electric field due to a uniformly charged infinite line of linear charge density $\lambda$, at a perpendicular distance $r$. Explain the choice of Gaussian surface, and contrast the distance dependence with that of a point charge and an infinite sheet.
questions.solution:
**Symmetry first.** An infinite uniformly charged line looks the same from any point at the same perpendicular distance, and the same in either direction along its length. So the field must:

- point **radially** outward (for positive $\lambda$), perpendicular to the line;
- have a magnitude depending **only on $r$**.

Any component along the line would have to point one way or the other, and there is nothing to choose between the two directions — so it is zero.

**Choosing the Gaussian surface.** Take a **cylinder** of radius $r$ and length $l$, coaxial with the line. This is the right choice because it matches the symmetry: $\vec{E}$ is perpendicular to the curved surface everywhere and constant in magnitude on it, and parallel to the two flat ends.

**The flux.**

Curved surface: $\vec{E}$ is parallel to $d\vec{A}$, so the flux is $E \times (2\pi r l)$.

Flat ends: $\vec{E}$ is perpendicular to $d\vec{A}$, so $\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0$ and they contribute **nothing**.

$\Phi = E(2\pi r l)$

**The enclosed charge.**

$q_{\text{enc}} = \lambda l$

**Applying Gauss's law.**

$E(2\pi r l) = \dfrac{\lambda l}{\varepsilon_0}$

The length $l$ cancels — as it must, since an infinite line has no special length:

$\boxed{E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}}$

Often written $E = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}$.

**Comparing the three geometries.**

Point charge: $E \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$

Infinite line: $E \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$

Infinite sheet: $E$ is **constant**, independent of distance.

The pattern is not a coincidence. Field lines from a point spread in three dimensions, so they thin out as $1/r^{2}$ (the area of a sphere). From a line they spread in only two dimensions, thinning as $1/r$ (the circumference of a circle). From a sheet they cannot spread at all, so the field never weakens.

**A caution.** This is an idealisation. A real charged wire behaves like this only close to it, at distances small compared with its length — far away it looks like a point charge and reverts to $1/r^{2}$.
